opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the main motivation was really simplicity. When DeepSeek R1 came out, there was this impression that you needed large-scale reinforcement learning, with lots of compute and a fairly complex pipeline, to get these strong reasoning capabilities. We wanted to ask: what's the simplest possible recipe that gets you test-time scaling and strong reasoning performance?

It turned out you can get surprisingly far with just supervised fine-tuning on a very small, carefully curated dataset. In our case it was about a thousand examples. We picked them for quality, difficulty, and diversity, with reasoning traces distilled from a strong reasoning model. Training on that took something like 26 minutes on 16 H100s, so it's extremely cheap compared to an RL pipeline.

I think part of the insight is that the base model, in our case Qwen 2.5 32B Instruct, already has a lot of the reasoning ability latent from pretraining. Fine-tuning mostly teaches it the format, to think for a long time, check its work, and backtrack. You don't necessarily need RL to unlock that if you have good demonstrations.

Then for controlling test-time compute, we added "budget forcing." If you want the model to think more, you suppress the end-of-thinking token and append something like "Wait," which often makes it re-examine and fix its answer. If you want it to think less, you cut it off and force an answer. That gave us a clean way to show performance scaling with more thinking tokens.

To be clear, I don't think RL is unnecessary in general. It's very powerful, especially if you want to go beyond what a teacher model can do. But for showing a minimal, reproducible, fully open recipe, SFT was the natural choice, and it makes it much easier for others to build on.

r002.rationale: It says simplicity was the main motivation and describes SFT as the natural choice for a minimal, reproducible recipe.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that the goal of s1 was sample efficiency and simplicity, and supervised fine-tuning turned out to be the most direct path to that.

When we started, the big open question after o1 was: what is the minimal recipe that gets you test-time scaling, where a model gets better the longer it thinks? A lot of people assumed you needed large-scale RL, and that is what DeepSeek R1 ended up showing works at scale. But we wanted to ask a different question, which is: how little data do you actually need? And for that question, SFT is just much easier to reason about. You pick a thousand examples, you fine-tune for a few minutes on a handful of GPUs, and you can look at exactly what the model saw.

The other piece is that we had a strong base model, Qwen2.5-32B, which already had a lot of the reasoning ability latent in it. Our hypothesis was that we didn't need to teach it to reason from scratch, we needed to elicit a behavior it was already capable of, namely producing long chains of thought with backtracking and verification. For eliciting a format or a style, a small amount of high-quality supervised data is very effective. We spent most of our effort on curating that data, filtering for difficulty, diversity, and quality, rather than on the training algorithm.

And then the test-time scaling part came from budget forcing, which is almost embarrassingly simple. You either cut off the thinking when it goes over budget, or you append "Wait" to make the model keep going, and that is enough to get a scaling curve. RL wasn't necessary for that mechanism to work.

I'd add that RL and SFT aren't really in opposition here. I think of what we did as a strong, cheap baseline, and RL on top of a model like s1 is a natural next step. It's just that for understanding the core phenomenon, SFT on a thousand examples was the cleanest experiment.

r002.rationale: It says simplicity was a goal and that supervised fine-tuning was the most direct, clean experimental approach.

astra-6.text:
We wanted to see how far we could get with the simplest possible approach. With supervised fine-tuning, you take examples of a reasoning process and train the model to imitate them. That gives you a straightforward way to test whether a small amount of carefully selected data can teach the behavior you want.

Reinforcement learning introduces more moving parts: you need a reward signal, you need to generate rollouts, and you need to make that training work reliably. It can be very powerful, but it wasn’t necessary for the question we were trying to answer with S1. We wanted a simple, accessible baseline for studying reasoning and test-time compute. That doesn’t mean supervised fine-tuning is ultimately better than reinforcement learning; it means we wanted to establish how much you could achieve before adding that complexity.

sol-6.1.text:
We wanted to see how far we could get with the simplest possible approach. Reinforcement learning introduces a lot of moving parts and can be expensive to reproduce. With supervised fine-tuning, we could take a small set of high-quality reasoning traces and directly teach the model that behavior.

For s1, we used just 1,000 examples. The idea wasn’t that supervised fine-tuning is necessarily better than reinforcement learning, but that it gives us a simple, reproducible way to study reasoning and test-time scaling. Then, with budget forcing, we could control how long the model thinks at inference time without adding a reinforcement-learning stage.
